reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design - Part 2: Ground investigation and testing

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Heading for the scope clauses: the scope of Eurocode 7 as a whole (1.1.1) and of EN 1997-2, ground investigation and testing (1.1.2).
sections.body: Heading for 1.1.1 and 1.1.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 10)
sections.applicability: Defines the scope, purpose, and boundary of EN 1997-2 relative to EN 1997-1 for all ground investigation and testing work.

sections.title: Scope of Eurocode 7
sections.summary: EN 1997 is used with EN 1990 (basis of design) for the geotechnical aspects of buildings and civil works, covering strength, stability, serviceability and durability, not thermal or sound insulation. Actions come from EN 1991, but ground-imposed actions such as earth pressures follow EN 1997; execution is covered only as far as design assumptions need; seismic design is in EN 1998.
sections.body: (1) EN 1997 is used together with EN 1990:2002, which sets the principles and requirements for safety and serviceability, the basis of design and verification, and structural reliability. (2) It applies to the geotechnical aspects of the design of buildings and civil engineering works and is split into parts (1.1.2). (3) It covers strength, stability, serviceability and durability; other requirements such as thermal or sound insulation are not considered. (4) Numerical values of actions are given in EN 1991, but actions imposed by the ground, such as earth pressures, shall be calculated by the rules of EN 1997. (5) Execution and workmanship are treated in separate European Standards named in the relevant sections. (6) Execution is covered only as far as needed to conform to the design rules' assumptions. (7) Special seismic requirements are not covered; EN 1998 adds rules for geotechnical seismic design. (p. 10)
key_points: EN 1997 is used with EN 1990:2002 (p. 10).
Earth pressures and other ground-imposed actions are calculated by EN 1997's rules (p. 10).
Seismic design is not covered; EN 1998 adds the rules (p. 10).
sections.applicability: Defines the scope, purpose, and boundary of EN 1997-2 relative to EN 1997-1 for all ground investigation and testing work.

sections.title: Scope of EN 1997-2
sections.summary: EN 1997-2, used with EN 1997-1, adds rules on planning and reporting ground investigations, general requirements for common laboratory and field tests, interpretation of results and derivation of geotechnical parameters, with examples of applying field tests to design. Characteristic values are in EN 1997-1. It targets geotechnical category 2; category 3 needs at least as much, often more.
sections.body: (1) EN 1997-2 is used with EN 1997-1 and gives supplementary rules on planning and reporting ground investigations; general requirements for a number of commonly used laboratory and field tests; interpretation and evaluation of test results; and derivation of values of geotechnical parameters and coefficients; with examples of applying field test results to design. Establishing characteristic values is covered in EN 1997-1. (2) No specific provisions are given for environmental ground investigations. (3) Only commonly used tests are covered, chosen for their importance in practice, availability in commercial laboratories and an accepted European procedure (p. 10); the laboratory tests on soils mainly apply to saturated soils, and later updates are expected to add tests. (4) The provisions apply primarily to geotechnical category 2 projects (2.1 of EN 1997-1:2004); category 1 investigations are normally limited because verification often rests on local experience; category 3 projects normally need at least the category 2 amount, and additional investigations and more advanced tests may be needed. (5) Derivation of parameter values is aimed primarily at pile and spread foundation design from field tests, as detailed in Annexes D to G (p. 11). (pp. 10 to 11)
key_points: Supplements EN 1997-1 on planning, reporting, testing, interpretation and derived values (p. 10).
Characteristic values are established by EN 1997-1, not EN 1997-2 (p. 10).
No specific provisions for environmental ground investigations (p. 10).
Laboratory tests on soils mainly apply to saturated soils (p. 11).
Aimed at geotechnical category 2; category 3 needs at least as much investigation (p. 11).
sections.applicability: Defines the scope, purpose, and boundary of EN 1997-2 relative to EN 1997-1 for all ground investigation and testing work.

sections.title: Normative references
sections.summary: Normative references: EN 1990:2002, EN 1997-1:2004, EN ISO 14688-1 and -2 and 14689-1 (soil and rock identification and classification), EN ISO 22475-1 (sampling and groundwater measurements) and EN ISO 22476 parts 1 to 9, 12 and 13 (field tests); CEN ISO/TS documents are in the Bibliography.
sections.body: (1) For dated references later amendments do not apply (parties are encouraged to check the latest editions); for undated references the latest edition applies. Listed: EN 1990:2002 Basis of structural design; EN 1997-1:2004 General rules; EN ISO 14688-1 and 14688-2 (identification and classification of soil); EN ISO 14689-1 (identification and description of rock); EN ISO 22475-1 (sampling by drilling and excavation and groundwater measurements); EN ISO 22476 field tests: part 1 electrical cone and piezocone, 2 dynamic probing, 3 standard penetration test, 4 Menard pressuremeter, 5 flexible dilatometer, 6 self-boring pressuremeter, 7 borehole jack, 8 full displacement pressuremeter, 9 field vane, 12 mechanical CPT, 13 plate loading test, several then 'to be published' (p. 11). NOTE: the Bibliography lists CEN ISO Technical Specifications for some tests; national standards may stay in force during a CEN ISO/TS's life, and National Annexes may give national practice (p. 12). (pp. 11 to 12)
key_points: Field tests refer to EN ISO 22476 parts (CPT, DP, SPT, PMT, FDT, SBP, borehole jack, FVT, plate test) (p. 11).
Sampling and groundwater measurement refer to EN ISO 22475-1 (p. 11).
Soil and rock identification refer to EN ISO 14688 and 14689 (p. 11).
sections.applicability: Identifies the companion standards that EN 1997-2 relies on for execution procedures of each sampling and test method.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.summary: The provisions assume, with EN 1990 and EN 1997-1 1.3, that design data are collected, recorded and interpreted by qualified personnel, structures are designed by qualified and experienced personnel, and continuity and communication exist between investigation, design and construction staff.
sections.body: (1) Reference is made to EN 1990:2002, 1.3 and EN 1997-1:2004, 1.3. (2) The provisions assume that data for design are collected, recorded and interpreted by appropriately qualified personnel; structures are designed by appropriately qualified and experienced personnel; and adequate continuity and communication exist between the people involved in data collection, design and construction. (p. 12)
key_points: Data collected, recorded and interpreted by qualified personnel (p. 12).
Continuity and communication between data collection, design and construction (p. 12).
sections.applicability: General personnel-competence and process-continuity assumptions underlying the validity of EN 1997-2's provisions.

sections.title: Distinction between Principles and Application Rules
sections.summary: Principles (marked P) are statements, definitions, requirements and models without alternative unless stated; Application Rules (numbered in brackets) are recognised rules satisfying them. Alternatives to Application Rules are allowed if shown equivalent, but the design then cannot claim full accordance with EN 1997-2 and may not suit CE marking.
sections.body: (1) Clauses are either Principles or Application Rules. (2) Principles are general statements and definitions with no alternative, and requirements and analytical models with no alternative unless specifically stated; (3) they carry the letter P. (4) Application Rules are generally recognised rules that follow the Principles and satisfy their requirements. (5) Alternatives to Application Rules are permitted if shown to accord with the Principles and to be at least equivalent for structural safety, serviceability and durability; NOTE: the design then cannot be claimed wholly in accordance with EN 1997-2, though it stays in accordance with the Principles of EN 1997-1, and for products under an Annex Z of a product standard an alternative may not be acceptable for CE marking (p. 12). (6) Application Rules are identified by a number in brackets (p. 13). (pp. 12 to 13)
key_points: Principles carry the letter P and admit no alternative unless stated (p. 12).
Application Rules are numbered in brackets, e.g. (1) (p. 13).
Alternatives to Application Rules need shown equivalence and lose full accordance with EN 1997-2 (p. 12).
sections.applicability: How to read EN 1997-2 clauses: Principles versus Application Rules

sections.title: Specific definitions used in EN 1997-2
sections.summary: Fifteen definitions: derived value (from test results by theory, correlation or empiricism), disturbed and undisturbed sample, measured value, natural, remoulded, re-compacted, reconstituted and re-consolidated specimen, quality class (five classes), remoulded sample, sample, specimen, strength index test, and swelling.
sections.body: 1.5.3.1 derived value: a geotechnical parameter value obtained from test results by theory, correlation or empiricism (1.6). 1.5.3.2 disturbed sample: soil structure, water content and/or constituents changed during sampling. 1.5.3.3 measured value: measured in a test. 1.5.3.4 natural specimen: made from the available (disturbed, undisturbed, remoulded) sample. 1.5.3.5 quality class: classification of a soil sample's quality in the laboratory; NOTE: five quality classes (3.4.1). 1.5.3.6 remoulded sample: soil or rock structure fully disturbed. 1.5.3.7 remoulded specimen: fully disturbed, at natural water content (p. 13). 1.5.3.8 re-compacted specimen: forced into a mould with a rammer or under a desired static stress. 1.5.3.9 reconstituted specimen: prepared in the laboratory, for fine soils as a slurry at or above the liquid limit then consolidated, for coarse soils poured or pluviated dry or wet and compacted or consolidated. 1.5.3.10 re-consolidated specimen: compressed in a mould or cell under static pressure with drainage. 1.5.3.11 sample: soil or rock recovered by sampling. 1.5.3.12 specimen: the part of a sample used for a test. 1.5.3.13 strength index test: indicates shear strength without necessarily a representative value; NOTE: results are uncertain. 1.5.3.14 swelling: expansion from reduced effective stress, by reduced total stress or water absorption at constant total stress, the reverse of compression and consolidation. 1.5.3.15 undisturbed sample: no change in soil characteristics of practical significance (p. 14). (pp. 13 to 14)
key_points: Derived value: from test results by theory, correlation or empiricism (p. 13).
Soil samples fall in five laboratory quality classes (3.4.1) (p. 13).
Reconstituted fine-soil specimens start as a slurry at or above the liquid limit (p. 14).
Strength index test results are subject to uncertainty (p. 14).
Undisturbed sample: no change of practical significance in soil characteristics (p. 14).
sections.applicability: Provides the controlled vocabulary used throughout EN 1997-2 for sample/specimen types and derived-value terminology.

sections.title: Test results and derived values
sections.summary: Test results and derived values are the basis for selecting characteristic values (EN 1997-1 2.4.3). Design runs from investigation and testing (EN 1997-2) to characteristic values and verification (EN 1997-1) (Figure 1.1). Test results are curves or parameter values (Annex A); derived values come by theory, correlation or empiricism; the annex correlations come from the literature.
sections.body: (1) Test results and derived values form the basis for selecting characteristic values of ground properties per 2.4.3 of EN 1997-1:2004. NOTE 1: design proceeds through site investigation and testing (rules in this standard), then characteristic values, then design verification, the last two in EN 1997-1 (Figure 1.1: field and laboratory test results and correlations give derived values, which with information from other sources form the geotechnical model and characteristic values; partial factors then give design values) (pp. 14 to 15). (2) Test results can be experimental curves or parameter values; Annex A lists test results as a reference to the test standards. (3) Derived values of parameters or coefficients come from test results by theory, correlation or empiricism. NOTE 2: the correlations in the annexes to Section 4 come from the literature, linking a parameter to a test result such as the CPT qc, or by theory (e.g. phi' from pressuremeter results or from the plasticity index). NOTE 3: sometimes the correlation is applied after the test results are corrected or transformed into conservative estimates, not before the characteristic value (p. 15). (pp. 14 to 15)
key_points: Test results and derived values are the basis for characteristic values (EN 1997-1, 2.4.3) (p. 14).
Characteristic and design values are covered by EN 1997-1 (p. 15).
Derived values come from test results by theory, correlation or empiricism (p. 15).
Annex correlations to Section 4 are taken from the literature (p. 15).
figures: Figure 1.1: General framework for the selection of derived values of geotechnical properties
sections.applicability: Defines how raw test results become derived parameter values and where that fits in the overall geotechnical design process shared with EN 1997-1.

sections.title: The link between EN 1997-1 and EN 1997-2
sections.summary: Figure 1.2 shows the architecture of CEN standards linked to EN 1997: EN 1997-1 holds design rules, EN 1997-2 ground investigation rules, test specifications, derivation of ground properties and example calculation methods for spread and deep foundations; test standards (CEN/TC 341) and execution standards (CEN/TC 288) complete it.
sections.body: (1) Figure 1.2 shows the general architecture of CEN standards for geotechnical engineering linked to EN 1997. EN 1997-1 covers design (framework, ground parameters, characteristic and design values, general site investigation rules, design of main structure types, execution assumptions). EN 1997-2 gives rules for ground investigations and for obtaining parameter or coefficient values used to determine characteristic values, and informative examples of calculation methods for spread and deep foundations. Implementing EN 1997 also needs other standards, notably test standards (CEN/TC 341: drilling, sampling and groundwater measurement, laboratory and field tests, tests on structures, identification and classification) and execution standards (CEN/TC 288) (pp. 15 to 16). (pp. 15 to 16)
key_points: EN 1997-1 holds design rules; EN 1997-2 investigation and testing rules (p. 15).
EN 1997-2 gives informative calculation examples for spread and deep foundations (p. 15).
Test standards come from CEN/TC 341, execution standards from CEN/TC 288 (p. 16).
figures: Figure 1.2: General architecture of the CEN standards linked with EN 1997
sections.applicability: Clarifies the division of labor between EN 1997-1 (design) and EN 1997-2 (investigation/testing) and their shared supporting standards.

sections.title: Symbols and units
sections.summary: Symbols (notation per ISO 3898:1997) in Latin and Greek letters for strength, compressibility, consolidation, particle size, moduli and field test results such as qc, N, (N1)60 and the dilatometer and pressuremeter quantities, with abbreviations of the tests; recommended units include kN, kNm and kPa.
sections.body: (1) Symbols for EN 1997-2, notation based on ISO 3898:1997: Latin letters (e.g. Cc compression index, c' effective cohesion intercept, cfv field vane undrained strength, cu undrained shear strength, Cs swelling index, cv coefficient of consolidation, Calpha secondary compression, D10 to D85 particle sizes, E, E' and test moduli such as E_FDT) (p. 16), Greek letters and test result symbols such as qc and (N1)60, and abbreviations for the tests. (2) Recommended units for geotechnical calculations include kN, kNm and kPa and their multiples. (pp. 16 to 19)
key_points: Notation follows ISO 3898:1997 (p. 16).
Recommended units include kN, kNm and kPa (p. 19).
sections.applicability: Reference symbol table for interpreting every equation and correlation elsewhere in the standard.
